body.heading: Celebrating the lightest day
paragraphs: Around the summer solstice, the longest day of the year, northern countries celebrate with an enthusiasm that only makes sense if you have lived through their winters. Sweden's Midsummer is the grand example: a maypole raised and danced around, wreaths of wildflowers worn, and tables of new potatoes, herring, and strawberries eaten outdoors whatever the weather attempts.
Flower crowns are serious business. Traditionally, young people gathered seven kinds of flowers — in some tellings, in silence, from seven meadows — to place under the pillow and dream of the future.

body.heading: Bonfires against the dark that returns
paragraphs: In many parts of Europe, midsummer bonfires are lit on hills and beaches. The light is celebrated at its peak partly because everyone knows it turns from here; the festival holds joy and a little defiance in the same hand.

Food, swimming, and staying up far too late are near-universal features. In Finland, Midsummer is a great migration to lakeside cottages, saunas, and bonfires by the water — the city empties and the countryside fills.

body.heading: Borrow the spirit, if not the latitude
paragraphs: Far from the north, the longest day still deserves marking: an outdoor meal eaten slowly, flowers on the table, a fire or candles at dusk, and permission to stay up and watch the light go. The festival's heart is noticing the year's turning while it happens.
Watch the sunset time together and stay out for it. On the longest day, dusk arrives like a rumour, and being there for it is the entire ceremony.
